diagnostic_evidence.quote: The improved noise dependence to $\frac{n}{m}\|\sigma\|^2_{L^2_\nu}$ can be obtained for free by performing the same estimates above \cite[Eq. (4.5)]{cohen2017optimal} without the last inequality.

issues.failure_explanation: With one evaluation per point and w=n/Phi_n, the noise contribution is (1/m^2) sum_i w^2 sigma^2 Phi_n(x_i). Its nu-expectation is (n/m)||sigma||^2_{L^2_mu}; the paper's own computation (lo904) gives E_nu[w^2 sigma^2 Phi_n] = n||sigma||^2_{L^2_mu}, and (eq2) shows this is also a lower bound up to cond. The quantity ||sigma||^2_{L^2_nu} = int sigma^2 Phi_n/n dmu can be smaller by a factor of about n. Example: V_n is piecewise constants with one cell of mu-measure about 1 and n-1 tiny cells, and sigma is supported on the large cell. That cell's coefficient is averaged over about m/n samples, so its error is about n sigma^2/m, while the stated bound gives about sigma^2/m. Carrying out CM17 (4.5) 'without the last inequality' yields the L^2_mu norm. The intro sample-complexity statement and the comparison chain in Remark rem:compare rest on the wrong baseline. That chain applies Jensen to reach ||sigma||^2_{L^2_nu}, and its '\simeq' silently drops (1/m)||sigma||^2_{L^2_mu}, which can dominate.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace ||sigma||^2_{L^2_nu} by ||sigma||^2_{L^2_mu} in Theorem thm:cm17 and in the introduction. In Remark rem:compare, compare via Cauchy-Schwarz: (1/m)||sigma||^2_{L^2_mu} + (1-1/m)||sigma sqrt(Phi_n/n)||^2_{L^1_mu} <= ||sigma||^2_{L^2_mu>. Remove the '\simeq' step.
issues.overall_effect: The stated baseline guarantee is false in general. The motivating claim m >~ n max{log n, ||sigma||^2_{L^2_nu}/eta} and the quantitative improvement argument in Remark rem:compare are unsupported as written. Theorem thm:main itself is unaffected.
issues.title: Noise term of the Christoffel least-squares baseline uses the L^2_nu norm where the L^2_mu norm is correct
issues.why_classification: A stated theorem is wrong by up to a factor of n, and the motivating comparison must be rederived. However, a short corrected statement plus a Cauchy-Schwarz argument restores the paper's improvement claim, with no new architecture.

issues.failure_explanation: U(p) = sum_i Lm p_i/(w(x_i) sigma^2(x_i)) R_i R_i^T, so the stated dependence with weights 1/sigma^2 does not keep U, and hence H, unchanged. More substantively, a linear dependence among the R_i R_i^T gives no control of sum_i a_i. Moving along a then generally leaves the simplex constraint ||q||_1 = 1, so the perturbed point need not be feasible. The proof never shows why a feasible, objective-preserving direction exists. One valid argument: at an optimum, sum a_i must vanish, because otherwise rescaling strictly lowers H, since H(cp) = H(p)/c. This step is missing.

failure_location.quote: Applying a perturbation argument for $\bm q^{*}_n$ along $\bm a$ yields another optimal solution that has a smaller $\delta$-support.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use weights 1/(w(x_i) sigma^2(x_i)). Add the homogeneity argument showing that sum a_i = 0 at an optimum, so that moving along a stays in P_m(delta) with U fixed. Alternatively, cite the standard Caratheodory result for A-optimal designs.
issues.overall_effect: The (n^2+n)/2 sparsity bound (spt) is not proved as written. Convexity, existence of a minimizer, and all downstream error bounds are unaffected.
issues.title: Support-reduction argument for the sparse A-optimal allocation does not preserve feasibility or the information matrix
issues.why_classification: A short local argument restores the stated bound exactly. No other result depends on the sparsity claim.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \E_{\bm y}[\|\widehat{\bm\alpha}(\bm p)-\bar{\bm\alpha}\|_2^2\mid \XX]\geq \frac{G(\bm p)}{\|\bm V^\top\bm W\bm V\|_2^2}
\tr(\bm U(\bm p)^{-1}),\quad\quad \bm U(\bm p) \coloneq \bm V^\top\bm W^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm\Sigma(\bm p)^{-1}\bm W^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm V

issues.failure_explanation: Gauss-Markov bounds H(p*) only by the variance of the non-reweighted estimator. By (eq1)-(eq2), that variance lies between G/||V^T W V||^2 and ||(V^T W V)^{-1}||^2 G; it is not G itself. Counterexample: if w sigma^2 is constant, then Sigma = cI, H = c tr((V^T W V)^{-1}) and G = c tr(V^T W V). If all eigenvalues of V^T W V equal 0.81 (allowed on the event A), then H = cn/0.81 > G = 0.81cn. Off A, H is not controlled, so the unconditional claim E_X[H(q*)] <= E_X[G(p*)] is unsupported. The claim that HLS-2's variance term is at most HLS-1's is therefore not established.

failure_location.quote: so that $H(\bm q^{*}_n)\leq H(\bm p^*_n)\leq G(\bm p^*_n)$ (the first inequality follows from the definition of $\bm q_n^*$ and the second uses the Gauss--Markov theorem)

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the claim with E[H(q*)|A] <= 0.9^{-4} E[G(p*)|A], using the conditional version in Theorem thm:main part 2. The comparison then holds up to an absolute constant.
issues.overall_effect: The stated comparison showing that the reweighted variant does not worsen the variance term is unproved as written. It holds only up to a constant factor and conditionally on A.
issues.title: False inequality H(p*) <= G(p*) attributed to Gauss-Markov in comparing HLS-2 with HLS-1
issues.why_classification: A local constant-factor correction with conditioning on A preserves the qualitative comparison and every formal result.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Choosing $l\geq \log(1/\delta)/\log 2$ and noting $2/\log 2<3$ yields the desired result.
The proof is finished by applying a similar boosting argument in Theorem \ref{thm:rb} to lift the constant probability in both cases to $1-\delta$.

issues.failure_explanation: The argument needs l disjoint blocks of k functions, with integer l >= log(1/delta)/log 2, so it needs n >= k ceil(log_2(1/delta)). The hypothesis does not imply this. For delta = 0.9 it only gives n > 0.16k, so not even one block of size k exists and the Markov step is unavailable. For log(1/delta) = 1.5 it needs n >= 3k but only gives n > 2.25k. Theorem thm:984 has the same defect: n > 10 log(1/delta) k versus ceil(log(1/delta)/log(10/9)) blocks of size 2s <= k.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require n >= k ceil(log_2(1/delta)) in thm:rb and n >= k ceil(log(1/delta)/log(10/9)) in thm:984, or equivalently n >= k(1 + C log(1/delta)).
issues.overall_effect: The probability-1-minus-delta guarantees of Theorems thm:rb and thm:984 are unproved for ranges of delta where rounding matters.
issues.title: Boosting hypothesis n > 1.5 log(1/delta) k does not guarantee enough disjoint blocks
issues.why_classification: A routine change to the hypothesis preserves the rates and conclusions.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where the last step holds if choosing $s = c'r(\log r)^3$

issues.failure_explanation: For r = 1 we get k = 0, so the space of sparse combinations with at most k terms is {0}. The theorem would then assert ||f|| <= 24 sqrt(tau_2) for every n. This is false when ||f|| is large and the KL tail tau_2 is small. The proof's own requirements, s > 2r+1 and s = c' r (log r)^3 (which equals 0 at r = 1), are incompatible there.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace log r by log(r+1) or max{1, log r} in the definitions of k and s.
issues.overall_effect: The stated sparse-approximation bound fails at the boundary case r = 1. It is otherwise unaffected.
issues.title: Theorem thm:984 degenerates for r = 1 because k = ceil(C_1 r (log r)^3) = 0
issues.why_classification: Fixing this degenerate parameter case is a one-line, standard change that keeps the rate and conclusion.
